query: For reported HfNbTiVAl10 with a hierarchical heterostructure, what testable hypothesis could enable Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture-related behavior to be predicted more rapidly and accurately under tensile and fracture testing than with established simulations? State the hypothesized rationale, the measurable gains in predictive accuracy and efficiency, circumstances in which the hypothesis may fail, relevant supporting evidence, and a predeclared result from independent measurements that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating quantitative microstructural descriptors of the hierarchical heterostructure in HfNbTiVAl10 into a physics‐informed, multiscale predictive model (combining first-principles derived parameters and machine learning regression) will allow faster and more accurate predictions of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior under tensile and fracture loading compared to established full-scale simulations.
generation.material_initial_state: HfNbTiVAl10 alloy in its as-processed state with a well‐characterized hierarchical heterostructure (e.g., phase boundaries, intragranular nanoprecipitates) as reported.
generation.intervention: Implement an integrated computational framework that fuses key microstructural descriptors (such as the spatial distribution and size of heterostructural features) with DFT‐informed parameters (e.g., misfit volumes, elastic constants, stacking fault energies) through a machine learning regression model.
generation.conditions: The approach is applied under standard, room-temperature tensile and fracture testing conditions with typical loading rates such that the microstructure remains unchanged during testing.
generation.structural_mediator: The hierarchical heterostructure (nano–and meso–scale features such as nanoprecipitates and phase interfaces) that govern local mechanical responses and dislocation interactions.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly incorporating microstructural parameters, the model can more directly capture the mechanisms of solid-solution and heterostructure-induced strengthening, which in turn govern elastic and plastic behavior; the physics‐informed machine learning model then accelerates the predictions by bypassing the computationally expensive full‐scale DFT or atomistic simulations.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in predictive error for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness by approximately 20–30% relative to conventional simulation techniques, along with a 5–10× decrease in computation time.
generation.baseline: Current established simulations based on DFT and continuum modeling that demand extensive computational resources and do not explicitly account for the hierarchical heterostructure details.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis may fail if the microstructural descriptors do not sufficiently capture the complex inelastic interactions or if the heterostructural features evolve (e.g., through phase transformations or thermal aging) under the testing conditions, thereby invalidating the initial model training.
generation.uncertainty: While the integration of microstructural features is expected to improve prediction efficiency and accuracy, the exact quantitative gains depend on the representativeness of the selected descriptors and the quality of the training data; thus, the improvements may vary, and further optimization might be required.

falsification_experiment.design: Develop the integrated physics-informed machine learning model using detailed microstructure data from HfNbTiVAl10. Conduct a series of controlled room-temperature tensile and fracture tests to obtain high-fidelity experimental measurements of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness. In parallel, predict these properties using both the new model and established simulations.
measurements: Young’s modulus from elastic region slopes of stress–strain curves
Yield strength determined by the 0.2% offset method
Fracture toughness derived from standardized fracture tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated model does not achieve a reduction of predictive error by at least ~20% relative to established simulation methods or fails to reduce simulation time by at least a factor of 5, then the hypothesis is decisively falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A typical method of choice for truly predictive calculations of alloy properties is density functional theory (DFT). However, explicit evaluation of fracture or yield strength in alloys is mostly out of reach for available DFT implementations. Although this may become possible with general-purpose interatomic potentials,, a fairly robust description can be obtained by using appropriate models, which have been shown to accurately predict strengthening and ductility. These models combine linear elasticity and microscopic principles, and the only required input parameters are certain material properties. Specifically, apart from basic equilibrium properties, such as the molar volume and elastic constants, the strengthening model requires misfit volumes related to concentration derivatives of the alloy volume, while the ductility model relies on surface and unstable stacking fault (USF) energies computed for specific orientations. Importantly, all of these parameters are accessible through simulations using first-principles methods, yet, such simulations are still challenging for disordered MPEAs.

Upon inspection of the fracture surface generated from in situ SEM microtensile testing (fig. S5), both faceted and dimpled regions are present, corresponding to brittle and ductile failure, respectively. Evidently, plastic deformation of the alloy occurs primarily through the ductile fcc phase, which has the aforementioned hierarchical architecture. Dislocation accumulation/storage is enhanced inside the fcc grains due to the presence of hierarchical intragranular nanoprecipitates, which may result in enhanced strain hardening and improved ductility () relative to other reported HEAs. This proposed mechanism accounts for the appreciable work hardening and failure strain of ~5.2% exhibited by the Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 HEA under tension at room temperature.
